cross_references.description: Section 1983 provides a statutory cause of action against state and local officers who violate constitutional rights. Bivens is the judge-made equivalent for federal officers. Section 1983 covers state actors; Bivens covers federal actors. Both allow suits for money damages against individual officers. Section 1983 remains robust and expanding. Bivens is functionally moribund.
cross_references.key_distinction: Section 1983 is statutory (Congress created it). Bivens is implied (the Supreme Court created it from the Constitution). Congress can expand Section 1983 at any time. Only the Supreme Court can expand Bivens, and it has refused to do so since 1980.

cross_references.description: Qualified immunity is the primary defense available to individual officers in both Section 1983 and Bivens suits. An officer is immune from damages unless the plaintiff can show the officer violated a 'clearly established' constitutional right — meaning a prior court decision with materially similar facts held the same conduct unconstitutional. The same qualified immunity standard applies whether the claim is brought under Section 1983 or Bivens.
cross_references.practical_effect: Even in the three surviving Bivens contexts, a plaintiff must overcome qualified immunity. The officer wins unless there is a prior case with nearly identical facts holding the conduct unconstitutional.

cross_references.description: The Federal Tort Claims Act (28 U.S.C. Sections 1346(b), 2671-2680) allows suits against the United States (not individual officers) for torts committed by federal employees acting within the scope of employment. After Egbert v. Boule (2022), the FTCA is often the only viable path for relief when federal officers cause harm, because the existence of the FTCA itself may block a Bivens claim.
cross_references.key_distinction: FTCA sues the government. Bivens sues the individual officer. FTCA has significant exceptions (discretionary function, intentional torts by non-law-enforcement officers). But where Bivens is unavailable, FTCA may be the only option.
